questions.scenario:
Gravity pulls straight down: (0, -9.8, 0). A character stands on a slope with normal ({{nx}}, {{ny}}, {{nz}}). How much of gravity pulls the character DOWN the slope? Give the magnitude (a positive scalar). Round to 2 decimals.
(Hint: The force down the slope = |gravity - projection of gravity onto normal|).
questions.solution: let d = gx*nx + gy*ny + gz*nz; let m = nx*nx + ny*ny + nz*nz; let s = d / m; let sx = gx - s*nx; let sy = gy - s*ny; let sz = gz - s*nz; sqrt(sx*sx + sy*sy + sz*sz)
hints: Remove the component of gravity that pushes INTO the slope (the normal component).
What's left is the component sliding down the slope.
Compute slide = gravity - (gravity·N)/(N·N) * N, then get its magnitude.

questions.scenario:
A forward-facing vector is ({{fx}}, {{fy}}, {{fz}}). An 'up' reference vector is ({{ax}}, {{ay}}, {{az}}). Compute the RIGHT vector using cross product. Normalize. Round to 3 decimals.
(Note: In a typical coordinate system, right = cross(down, forward). Use right = cross(forward, up) — but NORMALIZE the result).
questions.solution: let rx = fy*az - fz*ay; let ry = fz*ax - fx*az; let rz = fx*ay - fy*ax; let mag = sqrt(rx*rx + ry*ry + rz*rz); [rx/mag, ry/mag, rz/mag]
hints: Right = cross(forward, up) gives a vector perpendicular to both.
Compute cross product: (fy*uz - fz*uy, fz*ux - fx*uz, fx*uy - fy*ux).
Normalize by dividing by the magnitude.
